827.title: The fish who prayed for rain
827.hook: a fish king makes the rain fall by an act of truth (Jataka 75)
827.howItsDone: The act of truth appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too: in the Angulimala Sutta, Angulimala speaks a true sentence about his own life as a blessing for a woman in labor, and those words are chanted as a protective verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the virtuous elephant, sila itself, good to a man who came back with a saw. Your line: good to the ungrateful. Today, a new week, and a drought.

Cracked mud, in plates, where the water used to be. Each day the edge pulls back a little further. The fish crowd into what's left, and the crows and herons stand at the edge, waiting. In this Jataka tale, the Buddha in an earlier life is one of those fish, the king of the pond. He can't fly away or dig a well. He has one thing left to offer, and it isn't a plea or a bargain. It's a sentence that happens to be true.
screen: `THE MUD CRACKS INTO PLATES.` → `THE HERONS ARE WAITING.` → `ONE THING LEFT TO OFFER.`

segments.voice: First, the drought. The tale sets it in the kingdom of Kosala. No rain comes, the crops wither, and the pond goes to mud. The birds are picking the fish off one by one. Second, the fish king rises. He pushes up out of the mud, looks at the sky, and calls on Pajjunna, the god of the rain clouds in the story. But he doesn't ask for a favor. Third, the act of truth. In Pali it's called sacca-kiriya: a person states something true about their own life, sets it out like an offering, and the truth itself carries power. The fish king's truth: though he was born among fish, who eat one another, he has never, as far back as he can remember, taken the life of any creature. If that is true, he says, let the rain fall. And it does. The clouds gather, the pond fills, and the fish are saved. Fourth, why it matters. The act of truth only works because it's true. The fish can't bluff the sky; whatever power his words have comes from the life standing behind them. He doesn't promise to be good from now on, or describe the fish he hopes to be. He points to what he has already done, plainly, and lets it speak. Some readers hear a quiet question in the tale: what could you say about your own life that's simply true? Not impressive. Just true enough to stand on.

segments.voice: Feel the breath come and go a few times, then look for something about your life that's plainly true: I kept a promise this week; I'm tired today; I love my brother. Say it out loud, quietly, once, and sit with how it sounds in the room. Is it solid, or does it need anything added?

Your line: an act of truth. Plain, sure, and yours. That's day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: The forest of ogresses
828.hook: a prince crosses a forest of temptations without looking back (Jataka 96)
828.howItsDone: In Buddhist practice this is called guarding the sense doors: noticing a sight or a sound without being pulled after it, trained in both walking and sitting meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fish king's sacca-kiriya, one true sentence, and the rain came. Your line: an act of truth. Today, a road through a dangerous forest.

The road to the throne runs straight through a forest, and the forest is not empty. Along the way, the tale says, ogresses wait, and they don't look like monsters. They build pleasant houses by the road, spread soft couches, and call sweetly to anyone passing. A young prince sets out to cross it anyway, because holy men have told him one thing: keep walking, and don't look at them.
screen: `A ROAD THROUGH THE FOREST.` → `LOVELY HOUSES, SOFT COUCHES.` → `KEEP WALKING. DON'T LOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. The prince is told the ogresses will tempt travelers through every door of the senses: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touch. Whoever stops to look is lost. Second, the companions. A few men insist on coming, sure they can manage. One by one they fall behind: one for a lovely form, one for a song, one for a sweet scent, one for a fine meal, one for a soft bed. The ogresses take each of them. Third, the one who follows. The prince walks on alone. One ogress follows him all the way to the city, telling everyone she's his wife. He never so much as glances at her. She ends up in the king's palace, and the story turns dark for the king who took her in. The prince, who never turned his head, ends up on the throne. Fourth, the bowl of oil. The tale is called the Telapatta Jataka, the bowl-of-oil birth story, and it's linked to a teaching in the Samyutta Nikaya. There, a man must carry a bowl filled to the brim with oil through a crowd watching a famous beauty dance, while a man with a drawn sword walks behind him, ready to strike if a drop spills. The Buddha says the bowl stands for mindfulness of the body. Both stories make the same point. The trouble isn't that the lure is there; it's turning toward it. Attention is where the danger lies, and where the protection lies too.

segments.voice: Sit, and let something tempt you, a phone face down nearby, a snack in the kitchen, a plan for tomorrow, and when it calls, notice the picture, the sound, the pull. Don't turn your head; come back to the breath, steady and full, like the man carrying the oil. You can know the lure is there and still walk past it.

829.title: The tiger raised
829.hook: a student with a spell revives a dead tiger, which kills him (Jataka 150)
829.tomorrow: The donkey in the lion's skin
829.howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold in Buddhist sermons and children's classes, and a retelling often closes on the tale's verse, here the teacher's warning about whom we help back to their feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a prince crossed a forest of yakkhini without turning his head. Your line: don't look back. Today, a spell, and a tiger.

A spell for raising the dead. That's what a young student named Sanjiva has picked up from his teacher. Only half of it, though: the words that bring a body back to life, and not the words that would undo them. One day he's out in the forest with the other students, gathering wood, and they come across a dead tiger lying in the grass. Sanjiva has an idea. His friends have a different one.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` → `A DEAD TIGER IN THE GRASS.` → `SANJIVA HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: First, the half-learned spell. The tale says Sanjiva knew the charm for raising the dead but had never learned the charm for putting them down again: the start of something, and no way to finish it. Second, the boast. He tells his friends he'll bring the tiger back to life. They don't quite believe him, but they aren't foolish either. Before he begins, they climb up into the trees. Third, the waking. Sanjiva says the words. The tiger stirs, rises, and springs at the man who woke it. It kills him on the spot, and the tale says the tiger fell dead right there beside him. His friends come down and carry the news home. Fourth, the teacher's verse. The teacher, the Buddha in an earlier life, gives the tale its lesson: whoever helps a wicked one back to his feet is harmed by him, just as the tiger killed the one who raised it. The frame is about a king who took a schemer as his friend, so the warning first concerns companions. But the picture reaches further. Some things in a life are lying still for good reason: an old grudge, a habit that nearly sank you, an argument that finally went quiet. The words that wake them are easy to say. Putting them down again is the half of the spell that's easy to skip.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` · `FRIENDS CLIMB THE TREES.` · `THE TIGER WAKES AND SPRINGS.` · `DON'T RAISE THE WICKED.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WHAT YOU REVIVE.`

segments.voice: Let the mind wander a little, and watch what it tries to wake: an old argument, a grudge, a craving that had gone quiet. When one stirs, don't say the words that bring it to its feet; see it lying there, and leave it in the grass. Then come back to the breath.
Sanjiva. The student with half a spell, who revived a dead tiger in a Jataka tale, and was killed by it. Today's word.
Your line: careful what you revive. Waking is the easy half of the spell. Rest well.

830.title: The donkey in the lion's skin
830.hook: a donkey in a lion's skin is fine until he brays (Jataka 189)
830.howItsDone: In the Pali Canon, the Jataka's verses are the scripture and the prose stories come from the commentary told around them, so a retelling of this tale builds toward its verse about the bray.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sanjiva woke a tiger with half a spell. Your line: careful what you revive. Today, a disguise in a barley field.

There's a lion in the barley field. Or there seems to be. The watchmen see the tawny hide from the edge of the field and back away. Every day it's there again, head down, eating the crop, and the crop gets thinner, row by row. Nobody stops to wonder about one small thing. Odd, for a lion, to eat barley. This is the Sihacamma Jataka.
screen: `A LION IN THE BARLEY.` → `THE WATCHMEN BACK AWAY.` → `ODD, FOR A LION, TO EAT BARLEY.`

segments.voice: First, the trick. A traveling merchant carries his goods from village to village on a donkey. At each stop he unloads, throws a lion's skin over the donkey, and turns it loose in the fields. The watchmen keep their distance, and the donkey eats well. Second, the village rises. At one village, the watchmen have had enough. They rouse the people, who come out with drums and conch shells, shouting, heading for the field together. Third, the bray. Terrified by the noise, the donkey does the one thing a donkey can do. It brays, and the game is over. The villagers know a bray when they hear one. They fall on the donkey, and in the tale it is beaten to death in the field. The verse sums it up, in words close to these: that's no lion's roar, no tiger's, no panther's; it's a wretched donkey in a lion's skin. Fourth, what the tale is about. From a distance the skin fooled everyone. What gave the donkey away wasn't how it looked but its own voice, the moment fear pressed on it. Under pressure, what you are comes out, whatever you're wearing. Some readers add that the trouble was never being a donkey, a useful, honest thing to be that carries the load. The trouble started when it had to pass for a lion, and keep passing, until the day the drums came.
screen: `A LION'S SKIN ON A DONKEY.` · `THE VILLAGE COMES WITH DRUMS.` · `THE DONKEY BRAYS.` · `A DONKEY IS FINE TO BE.` · then, large: `THE BRAY GIVES IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Sit as you actually are today, not the version for work or for photos; find the posture you'd take if no one were looking. Let the breath go at its own pace, not a calm one you're performing, and if a thought comes about how you seem, let it pass. For these two minutes, there's no skin to hold up.
Siha. Lion: the name in the tale of a donkey's borrowed hide that fools the watchmen, until the drums come and the donkey brays. Today's word.
Your line: the bray gives it away. A donkey is a fine thing to be. Until tomorrow.

831.title: The woodpecker and the lion
831.hook: a woodpecker frees a bone from a lion's throat; the lion won't share (Jataka 308)
831.howItsDone: The Anguttara Nikaya names two kinds of people hard to find in the world: one who does a kindness first, and one who is grateful for it. In this tale the woodpecker is the first, and the lion is not the second.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a donkey in a siha's skin, a lion's, gave itself away with one bray. Your line: the bray gives it away. Today, a real lion, and a very small bird.

A lion lies in the forest and can't eat. While he was gulping down his kill, a bone lodged in his throat, and now it's swelling and the pain won't stop. A woodpecker on a branch above sees him suffering and flutters down to ask what's wrong. What is a bird supposed to do about a lion's throat? In the Javasakuna Jataka, quite a lot.
screen: `A BONE IN A LION'S THROAT.` → `A WOODPECKER ON A BRANCH.` → `WHAT CAN A BIRD DO?`

segments.voice: First, the stick. The woodpecker wants to help, but he isn't careless about it. A lion's mouth is no place to be. So he props the lion's jaws wide open with a stick, goes in, knocks the bone loose with his beak, comes back out and knocks the stick away. Second, the hungry day. Some time later the woodpecker can find nothing to eat. He comes across the lion feasting on a fresh kill, and asks, politely, for a little share. Third, the lion's answer. No. You've been inside a lion's mouth, the lion says, and come out alive. Let that be payment enough. Fourth, what the bird does next. A tree spirit living nearby asks the woodpecker why he doesn't strike back. He could peck at the lion's eyes. The woodpecker says no. Nothing good comes of harming someone who doesn't know what he owes. He'll simply go. And he flies off. A few days back, the elephant was good to a man who repaid him with a saw. This tale asks a smaller, everyday question: what about help that's just never thanked? The woodpecker shows two things. Help wisely, with a stick in the jaws, so your kindness doesn't get you eaten. And don't turn the help into a bill. He's still hungry when he flies away, and still free.

segments.voice: Choose someone who could use a hand, and find your stick: the one sensible precaution, a set time, a clear limit, a question asked first, that keeps the help from costing more than you can give. Your line: help anyway. Once it's given, it's given, and the bird flies off free. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: The preacher of patience
832.hook: an ascetic stays patient while a drunken king has his limbs cut (Jataka 313)
832.howItsDone: Patience, khanti, is one of the ten perfections in the Theravada tradition, and this tale is told as the Bodhisatta's practice of that perfection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a woodpecker freed a lion's throat, and wouldn't strike back. Your line: help anyway. Today, a hard tale, and a steady man at its center.

A king falls asleep in his pleasure garden, drunk, with his head in the lap of one of his women. The women of his court, bored with waiting, wander off through the trees and find an ascetic sitting quietly by himself. They sit around him and ask him to teach. When the king wakes and finds them gone, he goes looking, furious. A word of warning: this tale has violence in it, told plainly.
screen: `A KING ASLEEP, DRUNK.` → `HIS WOMEN FIND AN ASCETIC.` → `THE KING WAKES, FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The king demands to know what this ascetic teaches. Patience, he answers; in Pali, khanti. That's why the tale calls him Khantivadi, the preacher of patience. Second, the test. The king calls for his executioner. He has the ascetic flogged, and then, one cruelty after another, has his hands and feet cut off, then his ears and nose. After each, the king asks: what do you teach now? Each time the answer is the same. Third, where patience lives. The ascetic tells the king his patience isn't in his hands or feet, or any part of him a blade can reach. It lies deep within, in the heart. The king kicks him and walks away, and in the tale, as he leaves the garden, the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the last word. The king's commander comes back to the dying man and begs: if you must be angry, be angry with the king, not with the kingdom. The ascetic answers that he wishes the king long life, and that people like him do not get angry. Then he dies. The tale is very hard to hear, and it isn't advice to stay where you're being harmed. It's a picture of a quality pushed to its far edge: patience that doesn't live anywhere the world can cut. What tests an ordinary day is far smaller: a slow line, a loud neighbor, a careless remark. That's where the practicing happens.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU TEACH? PATIENCE.` · `THE KING TESTS IT.` · `NOT IN HANDS OR FEET.` · `MAY THE KING LIVE LONG.` · then, large: `PATIENCE HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and wait for one small irritation to arrive: a sound outside, an itch, a thought that you're wasting time. When it comes, don't fix it; feel where it pinches, and breathe toward that spot. See whether the patience lives in the itch, or somewhere further in.

Your line: patience holds. Not in the hands or the feet: in the heart. Day eight hundred thirty-two, done.

833.title: The sky is falling
833.hook: a hare hears a fruit fall and starts a stampede; a lion checks the facts (Jataka 322)
833.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching on right speech asks whether words are true, helpful and timely before they're spoken, and teachers sometimes use this tale to show how a rumor grows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the preacher of khanti, patience no blade could reach. Your line: patience holds. Today, a noise in the forest.

Thud. A hare is lying under a palm tree, near a grove of vilva trees, turning over an anxious thought: if the earth broke apart, what would become of me? Just then a ripe vilva fruit drops onto a dry palm leaf right beside him. Thud. He doesn't look round to see what it was. He's already running, and shouting as he goes. The old saying has the sky falling. In this Jataka tale, it's the earth.
screen: `AN ANXIOUS HARE.` → `A FRUIT DROPS ON A LEAF.` → `HE RUNS WITHOUT LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First, the run. The hare cries that the earth is breaking up. Another hare sees him running and runs too, without asking why. Then more hares, then deer and boars, buffaloes and tigers, even elephants, a whole forest pounding toward the sea. Second, the lion. A lion sees the stampede and asks the one question nobody has asked: who saw the earth breaking up? The elephants don't know; the tigers told them. The tigers point to others, and so on down the line, back to the hares, and the hares point at one hare. Third, the check. Where were you when you heard it, the lion asks. He takes the hare on his back and goes to the spot. There's the palm leaf, and the fruit lying on it. Fourth, the return. The lion goes back and tells the herd what he found, and the animals, who were running toward the sea, are saved. In the tale the lion is the Buddha in an earlier life, and his gift is not strength or speed: one question, and the patience to walk back and look. A frightening thing passes from mouth to mouth and grows as it goes. Everyone runs because someone else is running. Nobody goes back to the palm leaf.
screen: `THE WHOLE FOREST RUNS.` · `WHO SAW IT?` · `BACK TO THE PALM LEAF.` · `THE HERD IS SAVED.` · then, large: `CHECK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let the mind bring up one worry it's picked up from somewhere, passed along, half-heard, shared without a source, and watch how fast it wants to run. Then ask the lion's question: who saw it, and where's the palm leaf? No answer is needed now; just feel the difference between a thud and a falling world.
Palm leaf. What a lion found at the bottom of a rumor, a hare's fruit fallen onto a dry palm leaf, after the whole forest stampeded toward the sea. Today's word.
Your line: check first. The week in lines: an act of truth, don't look back, careful what you revive, the bray gives it away, help anyway, patience holds, check first. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're the lion, and the whole forest is stampeding past you toward the sea. what do you do?
options: run with them; they must know something.
ask who saw it, and go back to look.
roar to make them run faster.
fork.reveal: the lion traces the story back to one hare, carries him to the spot, finds the fruit on the palm leaf, and saves the herd.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nursery tale about panic.
what it means: one unchecked sound becomes a stampede, and one question stops it.
what a scholar hears: in the Jataka the hare fears the earth breaking up, not the sky, and the lion who checks is the Bodhisatta.
recall: the steady chant for reciting verses
guess: the small true cause behind a big scare
a sign that the earth is breaking up
a message passed from one hare to the next

chat.says: In the hare story, how did the lion stop the whole stampede?
options: He asked who saw it, traced it back, and went to look at the spot.
He roared so loudly that every animal froze and stopped running.
He told them the earth was fine, and they trusted the king of beasts.
chat.meaning: The lion asked who saw the earth breaking, traced the story back to one hare, and went to the palm leaf. Checking saved the herd.

vilva.meaning: a fruit tree; its ripe fruit fell on the palm leaf

Jataka.meaning: the collection of stories of the Buddha's past lives
